newsitem.title: THAILAND: Reuter Poll sees no early Thai recovery, growth dip.
newsitem.headline: Reuter Poll sees no early Thai recovery, growth dip.

text.p: Economists and analysts polled by Reuters this week did not expect to see a quick recovery for the battered Thai economy and did not expect government rescue measures to produce positive results soon.

Among the eight analysts from Thailand, Hong Kong and Singapore surveyed by Reuters, only one expected the economy, which is facing its worst slump in over a decade, to start showing signs of a pickup from the fourth quarter.

"The Thai economy is worse than expected and cannot recover in the short run," said Kasem Prunratanamala of HSBC James Capel Asia. He said the Thai central bank held the key to cuts in high Thai interest rates, blamed by business for stifling any economic rebound.
Most analysts trimmed their prjections of 1997 gross domestic product growth made in the first quarter.
Five out of eight now saw the economy growing by only up to five percent, the lowest in a decade, against actual 6.4 percent growth in 1996.
Official forecasts are for 5.9 percent growth this year.

An analyst at HSBC James Capel Asia said the economy may grow by only 3.0-3.5 percent in 1997, compared to the 4.3 percent he had expected early this year. A Deutsche Morgan Grenfell analyst also estimated 3.5-3.6 percent, against a 5.4 percent prediction earlier.
The rest of the poll contributors said the economy should expand 5.2-6.3 percent this year.
In a poll conducted in the first quarter, most analysts had expected 1997 GDP to grow 5.2-6.5 percent. A near unanimous

view emerging from the survey showed that the market attributed Thailand's weak economic outlook to sustained high interest rates, sluggish exports, an unstable baht and absence of effective central bank measures to deal with economic problems.
Thai prime lending rates of 12.75-13.50 percent are among the highest in the region and have forced liquidity crunches in Thailand's troubled finance and property sectors.

Philip Smyth of Asia Equity Ltd said the expected slow economic recovery and absence of stock market direction prompted him to advise clients to stay on the sidelines. Pipat Ronnakiart of Adkinson Securities Plc, however, expected the economy to show recovery signs from the fourth quarter when he saw room for interest rates to ease.
